title: Senior's toolkit: LINQ you can see
summary: Trying queries in LINQPad, inspecting them in the debugger, and the LINQ calls that avoid the classic crashes.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: LINQ you can see
steps.body: LINQ is easy to write and easy to get subtly wrong: a query that runs twice, a duplicate key that throws, a `Count()` that walks a million rows. Experienced developers try queries somewhere fast, look at the results in the debugger, and know the few calls that avoid those traps.

toolkit.what: A scratchpad for C#: paste a query, press F5, and `.Dump()` shows any object or sequence as a table. Many .NET developers keep it open all day to try queries before they go into the codebase.
flags: the language mode for a few lines of code
print with a heading; returns the value, so it can sit inside a chain

toolkit.what: A LINQ query is only a recipe until something enumerates it. In the debugger, expand the variable and then Results View to run it and see the items.
flags: runs the query now, in the debugger
anything the query does (logging, I/O) happens again when you expand it

toolkit.what: Run the query once and keep the results. Without it, every `foreach`, `Count()` or `Any()` on a query runs the whole pipeline again.
flags: the analyzer warning for possible multiple enumeration of an IEnumerable
return `IReadOnlyList<T>` from methods, not a lazy `IEnumerable<T>`, when callers will enumerate twice

toolkit.what: `ToDictionary` throws on a duplicate key; `ToLookup` groups items by key and allows many per key, and a missing key gives an empty sequence instead of an exception.
flags: one item per key: duplicates are a bug
many items per key, ready to index: `byCustomer[42]`
toolkit.example:
var ordersByCustomer = orders.ToLookup(o => o.CustomerId);
foreach (var o in ordersByCustomer[customer.Id]) Print(o);

toolkit.what: Get the item with the largest key, or drop duplicates by a key, without `OrderBy(...).First()` or a hand-written loop.
flags: the whole item with the largest total (first one on a tie)
keep the first item for each email
the old way: sorts everything, O(n log n)
toolkit.example:
var biggest = orders.MaxBy(o => o.Total);
var uniqueUsers = users.DistinctBy(u => u.Email.ToLowerInvariant());

toolkit.what: Ask "is there at least one?" with `Any()`, which stops at the first match. `Count() > 0` may walk the whole sequence.
flags: true as soon as one item exists
true as soon as one item matches
on a List or array, `.Count` / `.Length` is free

steps.prompt: The weekly report job crashes with this. The data has two rows for customer 42 since a merge. What is the right fix?
code: System.ArgumentException: An item with the same key has already been added. Key: 42
at System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary`2.TryInsert(TKey key, TValue value, InsertionBehavior behavior)
at System.Linq.Enumerable.SpanToDictionary[TSource,TKey](ReadOnlySpan`1 source, Func`2 keySelector, IEqualityComparer`1 comparer)
at System.Linq.Enumerable.ToDictionary[TSource,TKey](IEnumerable`1 source, Func`2 keySelector, IEqualityComparer`1 comparer)
options: Decide what a duplicate means: `ToLookup` (or `GroupBy`) if a customer can have several rows, or `DistinctBy` / fix the data if it must be one
Wrap line 27 in `try/catch` and skip the report
Replace `ToDictionary` with `ToList` and search it with `First`
Sort the rows first; `ToDictionary` then ignores duplicates
steps.explain: `ToDictionary` is a claim that keys are unique, and the exception says the data broke that claim. Either the model allows several rows per key (use a lookup) or the duplicate is bad data that should be fixed at the source.

steps.prompt: Queries are lazy. What does this print?
code: var people = new[] { (Name: "Ann", Age: 31), (Name: "Bo", Age: 45), (Name: "Cy", Age: 45) };
steps.explain: `big` runs when `Count()` is called, after 10 was added, so it sees 2, 3 and 10. `MaxBy` returns the first item with the largest key, so Bo, not Cy.

steps.prompt: Match each call to what it gives you.
pairs: one item per key; throws on a duplicate
several items per key; a missing key is empty
the whole item with the largest total
the first item for each email
runs the query once and keeps the results

steps.prompt: Index orders by customer so `byCustomer[id]` never throws, then find the biggest order.
steps.explain: `Max` returns only the largest total, not the order. `GroupBy` is lazy and has no indexer, and `ToDictionary` throws when a customer has two orders.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Try a tricky query in LINQPad or the Immediate window before it goes into the code. Every time you write `ToDictionary`, ask what happens on a duplicate key. When a query result is used more than once, put `ToList()` on it and say so with the return type.
